Q: What does PoissonRegression.predict() actually return in sklearn? A:

Here you can find a good example of the PoissonRegression https://scikit-learn.org/stable/auto_examples/linear_model/plot_poisson_regression_non_normal_loss.html

Short answer: PoissonRegression.predict() gives the prediction outputs. You are only confused because you use this kind of prediction if the target value is a value over time. In the example:

The number of claims (ClaimNb) is a positive integer that can be modeled as a Poisson distribution. It is then assumed to be the number of discrete events occurring with a constant rate in a given time interval (Exposure, in units of years).

Here we want to model the frequency y = ClaimNb / Exposure conditionally on X via a (scaled) Poisson distribution, and use Exposure as sample_weight.

So if you want to use PoissonRegression, the data should be poisson distributed

Q: How do I stabilise Sort-Object in PowerShell 5.1? A:

To sort the collection in a stable manner do the following:

  • Attach an index to each item in the collection.
  • Sort your collection and use the index as the last sorting criteria in ascending order.
  • Remove the index from each item.

In practice this could look like this:

1..20 `
  | ForEach-Object -Begin {$Index = 0} -Process {
      @{Index = $Index; Value = $_}
      $Index++
    } `
  | Sort-Object (
      @{Expression = { $_.Value % 2 }; Descending = $true},
      @{Expression = { $_.Index     }; Ascending  = $true}
    ) `
 | ForEach-Object {$_.Value}

Q: Using advisory locks to coordinate database activity A:

A SQLAlchemy Session isn't really a regular PostgreSQL session, and its .commit() doesn't just send a SQL commit. It cleans up the connection and hands it back to the pool, so you're losing your advisory lock.

Use a Connection instead of a Session, or acquire a Connection-bound Session.

From Basics of Using a Session:

Note that after Session.commit() is called, either explicitly or when using a context manager, all objects associated with the Session are expired, meaning their contents are erased to be re-loaded within the next transaction. If these objects are instead detached, they will be non-functional until re-associated with a new Session, unless the Session.expire_on_commit parameter is used to disable this behavior. See the section Committing for more detail.

Then, from Committing recommend above:

The Session.commit() operation unconditionally issues Session.flush() before emitting COMMIT on relevant database connections. If no pending changes are detected, then no SQL is emitted to the database. This behavior is not configurable and is not affected by the Session.autoflush parameter.

Subsequent to that, assuming the Session is bound to an Engine, Session.commit() will then COMMIT the actual database transaction that is in place, if one was started. After the commit, the Connection object associated with that transaction is closed, causing its underlying DBAPI connection to be released back to the connection pool associated with the Engine to which the Session is bound.

If your Session is bound to the Connection rather than an Engine, the last paragraph doesn't apply: you get to keep it, with the lock still in it.

What happened to your lock

My assumption was that it gets implicitly released by pg_advisory_unlock_all() in a discard all done by pool_reset_on_return='rollback':

"rollback" - call rollback() on the connection, to release locks and transaction resources. This is the default value.

But it seems that unless you set up a custom reset-on-return scheme for PostgreSQL dialect, SQLAlchemy doesn't do a full discard all so the lock release they're promising above only refers to regular, transaction-level, non-advisory locks, as a consequence of a simple plain SQL rollback this cleanup is limited to - and that doesn't affect advisories:

Unlike standard lock requests, session-level advisory lock requests do not honor transaction semantics: a lock acquired during a transaction that is later rolled back will still be held following the rollback, and likewise an unlock is effective even if the calling transaction fails later.

This would mean when you call session.commit(), the Connection holding the lock goes back into the pool, without releasing it. Not only do you lose the lock, this blocks you from re-acquiring.

  • If there's nothing else using that Engine and its pool, it's possible you can immediately get it back if you use_lifo.
  • In FIFO, you'll keep getting new ones until the pool expands to its target pool_size=5, then you'll get it back. This suggests another silly workaround would be to just keep committing.
  • You can also keep FIFO, but reduce pool_size=1 and max_overflow=0.
  • Funnily enough, if that Engine and pool are shared, the connection with the lock in it could happen to end up in hands of this other competing worker, precisely the one you wanted to block by doing all this.

Some pools routinely kill off connections and spawn new ones in their FIFO but SQLAlchemy's default QueuePool only does that when it operates above pool_size, up to pool_size+max_overflow, or if you tell it to recycle them on timeout.
